{{Short description|Inequality in mathematical analysis}}
In the field of [[mathematical analysis]], an '''interpolation inequality''' is an inequality of the form

:<math>
\| u_{0} \|_{0} \leq C \| u_{1} \|_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \| u_{2} \|_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \dots \| u_{n} \|_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}, \quad n \geq 2,
</math>

where for <math>0\leq k \leq n</math>,  <math>u_k</math> is an element of some particular vector space <math>X_k</math> equipped with norm <math>\|\cdot\|_k</math> and <math>\alpha_k</math> is some real exponent,  and <math>C</math> is some constant independent of <math>u_0,..,u_n</math>. The vector spaces concerned are usually [[Function space|function spaces]], and many interpolation inequalities assume <math>u_0 = u_1 = \cdots = u_n</math> and so bound the norm of an element in one space with a combination norms in other spaces, such as [[Ladyzhenskaya's inequality]] and the [[Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality]], both given below. Nonetheless, some important interpolation inequalities involve distinct elements <math>u_0,..,u_n</math>, including [[Hölder's inequality]] and [[Young's inequality for convolutions]] which are also presented below.

== Applications ==
The main applications of interpolation inequalities lie in fields of study, such as [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]], where various function spaces are used. An important example are the [[Sobolev spaces]], consisting of functions whose [[Weak derivative|weak derivatives]] up to some (not necessarily [[integer]]) order lie in [[Lp space|''L<sup>p</sup>'' spaces]] for some p. There interpolation inequalities are used, roughly speaking, to bound derivatives of some order with a combination of derivatives of other orders. They can also be used to bound products, convolutions, and other combinations of functions, often with some flexibility in the choice of function space. Interpolation inequalities are fundamental to the notion of an [[interpolation space]], such as the space <math>W^{s,p}</math>, which loosely speaking is composed of functions whose <math>s^{th}</math> order weak derivatives lie in <math>L^p</math>. Interpolation inequalities are also applied when working with [[Besov space|Besov spaces]] <math>B^s_{p,q}(\Omega)</math>, which are a generalization of the Sobolev spaces.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=DeVore|first1=Ronald A.|last2=Popov|first2=Vasil A.|date=1988|title=Interpolation of Besov spaces|url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1988-305-01/S0002-9947-1988-0920166-3/|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=305|issue=1|pages=397–414|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1988-0920166-3|issn=0002-9947|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Another class of space admitting interpolation inequalities are the [[Hölder condition#Hölder spaces|Hölder spaces]].

== Examples ==
A simple example of an interpolation inequality — one in which all the {{math|''u''<sub>''k''</sub>}} are the same {{mvar|u}}, but the norms {{math|‖·‖<sub>''k''</sub>}} are different — is [[Ladyzhenskaya's inequality]] for functions <math>u: \mathbb{R}^2 \rarr \mathbb{R}</math>, which states that whenever {{mvar|u}} is a [[compactly supported]] function such that both {{mvar|u}} and its [[gradient]] {{math|&nabla;''u''}} are square integrable, it follows that the [[fourth power]] of {{mvar|u}} is integrable and<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Foias|first1=C.|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/navierstokes-equations-and-turbulence/F183F2E2116DF34CE771B3622469BF22|title=Navier-Stokes Equations and Turbulence|last2=Manley|first2=O.|last3=Rosa|first3=R.|last4=Temam|first4=R.|date=2001|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-36032-6|series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511546754}}</ref>

:<math>
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}} | u(x) |^{4} \, \mathrm{d} x \leq 2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}} | u(x) |^{2} \, \mathrm{d} x \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}} | \nabla u(x) |^{2} \, \mathrm{d} x,
</math>

i.e.

:<math>
\| u \|_{L^{4}} \leq \sqrt[4]{2} \, \| u \|_{L^{2}}^{1/2} \, \| \nabla u \|_{L^{2}}^{1/2}.
</math>

A slightly weaker form of Ladyzhenskaya's inequality applies in dimension 3, and Ladyzhenskaya's inequality is actually a special case of a general result that subsumes many of the interpolation inequalities involving Sobolev spaces, the [[Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Evans |first=Lawrence C. |author-link=Lawrence C. Evans |title=Partial differential equations |date=2010 |isbn=978-0-8218-4974-3 |edition=2 |location=Providence, R.I. |pages= |oclc=465190110}}</ref>{{rp|pp=276-280}}

The following example, this one allowing interpolation of non-integer Sobolev spaces, is also a special case of the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Brézis|first=H.|author-link=Haïm Brezis|title=Functional analysis, Sobolev spaces and partial differential equations|date=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-70914-7|location=New York|pages=233|oclc=695395895}}</ref> Denoting the <math>L^2</math> Sobolev spaces by <math>H^k = W^{k,2}</math>, and given real numbers <math display="inline">1\leq k < \ell < m </math> and a function <math>u \in H^m</math>, we have

<math>\|u\|_{H^{\ell}}\leq \|u\|_{H^{k}}^{\frac{m-\ell}{m-k}} \|u\|_{H^{m}}^{\frac{\ell-k}{m-k}}.</math>


The elementary interpolation inequality for [[L^p space| Lebesgue spaces]], which is a direct consequence of the [[Hölder's inequality]]<ref name=":0" />{{rp|p=707}} reads: for exponents <math>1\leq p \le r  \le q\le \infty</math>, every <math>f\in L^p(X,\mu)\cap L^q(X,\mu)</math> is also in <math>L^r(X,\mu),</math> and one has

:<math>\|f\|_{L^r} \leq \|f\|_{L^p}^t \|f\|_{L^q}^{1-t},</math>

where, in the case of <math>p<q<\infty,</math>  <math>\frac{1}{r}</math> is written as a convex combination <math>\frac{1}{r}= \frac{t}{p} + \frac{1-t}{q}</math>, that is, with <math>t:=\frac{p(q-r)}{r(q-p)}</math> and  <math>1-t=\frac{q(r-p)}{r(q-p)}</math>; in the case of <math>p<q=\infty</math>, <math>r</math> is written as <math>r=\frac pt</math> with <math>t:=\frac pr</math> and <math>1-t=\frac{r-p}r.
</math>


An example of an interpolation inequality where the elements differ is [[Young's inequality for convolutions]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Leoni|first=Giovanni|title=A first course in Sobolev spaces|date=2017|isbn=978-1-4704-2921-8|edition=2|location=Providence, Rhode Island|oclc=976406106}}</ref> Given exponents <math>1\leq p,q,r \leq \infty</math>  such that <math>\tfrac{1}{p} + \tfrac{1}{q} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{r}</math> and functions <math>f \in L^{p}, \ g \in L^{q}</math>, their [[convolution]] lies in <math>L^r</math> and

:<math>\|f * g\|_{L^{r}} \leq \|f\|_{L^{p}} \|g\|_{L^{q}}.</math>
